name: Referral Systems & Primary Care
description: Iran’s primary care network connects community health workers with physician-led health centres and more specialized services. Its referral arrangements provide an organizational framework, but research documents persistent weaknesses in coordination, specialist feedback, and continuity of care.

seo.title: Referral Systems and Primary Care in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iran’s community health network, family physician programme, referral pathways, and documented barriers to coordinated care.

content.heading: Care begins close to home
content.content: Iran’s primary care network brings basic services into communities through village health houses and urban health posts. Rural community health workers, commonly called *behvarz*, connect households with the wider health system. Physician-led rural health centres provide another point of assessment and treatment, with referral onward when a patient needs specialist services. A WHO-hosted account describes corresponding urban arrangements involving health posts, health centres, and district hospitals. These are descriptions of the network’s organization, rather than a guarantee that every patient follows the same route. [s1](https://eurohealthobservatory.who.int/docs/librariesprovider3/publicationsnew/who-phc-book-2024-final-web-version-conference-copy.pdf?download=true&sfvrsn=695306e7_2)

content.heading: From community coverage to coordinated care
content.content:
The Family Physician Programme began in 2005 within a longer sequence of health-system reforms. Its significance lies in connecting first-contact care with subsequent treatment, rather than treating each consultation as an isolated event. The network distinguishes primary care from secondary services and the most specialized hospital care. This hierarchy can organize escalation, but the existence of facilities at successive levels does not itself establish reliable communication between them. [s1]

WHO’s 2020 assessment places Iran’s community health-worker approach within the broader pursuit of universal health coverage: access to needed services with financial protection. It describes reforms addressing insurance coverage, patient cost-sharing, benefit packages, and purchasing arrangements. These financing questions matter because a referral pathway must be usable and affordable as well as formally available. The assessment presents a reform agenda, not proof that all its objectives were achieved. [s3](https://www.who.int/publications-detail-redirect/978-92-4-000377-4)

content.title: The documented referral hierarchy
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Rural health house"] -->|"Referral for physician assessment"| C["Rural health centre"]
  B["Urban health post"] -->|"Referral within urban network"| D["Urban health centre"]
  C -->|"Referral for specialized care"| E["Secondary care services"]
  D -->|"Referral for specialized care"| E
  E -->|"Referral for more specialized care"| F["Tertiary hospital services"]
```
content.summary: Arrows represent referral relationships described in the source. They do not establish compulsory gatekeeping, insurance authorization, or consistent completion of referrals.

content.heading: Where the pathway breaks down
content.content:
A scoping review published in 2025 examined research on referral-system challenges through 2022. Its abstract identifies fragmented policies, weak oversight, delayed physician payments, and restrictive insurance tariffs. It also reports poor specialist feedback, low levels of referral back to primary care, and fragmented electronic records. These findings describe implementation problems across the reviewed evidence; they should not be read as a uniform assessment of every district in 2026. [s2](https://publish.kne-publishing.com/index.php/ijph/article/view/19852)

The review also identifies distrust of family physicians and rural specialist shortages as barriers. Its central implication is that expanding first-contact services alone cannot secure continuity: the subsequent consultation, transfer of information, and return to ongoing care also matter. Understanding Iran’s referral system therefore requires holding its organizational design and its documented operational limitations together. [s2]

name: Medical Services
description: Medical services in Iran span outpatient consultations, hospital treatment, diagnostic testing, rehabilitation, and care outside hospitals. Public, private, charitable, and employment-linked providers participate, with important differences in access and financing.

seo.title: Medical Services in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: An introduction to Iran’s consultation, treatment, diagnostic, and follow-up services, including provider differences and evidence gaps.

content.heading: A network of different services
content.content: Iran’s medical-service landscape extends beyond hospitals. WHO’s assessment of the private sector describes clinical care delivered through hospitals, clinics, polyclinics, and independent practices. Its clinical-pathway figure also includes diagnostic and treatment transitions, rehabilitation, nursing, and home care. A polyclinic brings multiple consultation services into one setting; an independent practice is a separate practitioner’s service. These distinctions help explain why a patient’s care may involve several organizations rather than one institution. [s1](https://www.ccpsh.org/sites/default/files/uploaded_files/2025-10/PSE%2520in%2520I.R.%2520Iran-eng.pdf)

content.heading: Who provides care, and who pays?
content.content:
Provider ownership and payment arrangements are separate questions. Alongside public and private providers, the Social Security Organization operates facilities and purchases services. It is therefore both a financing institution and a participant in service delivery. WHO’s assessment also identifies private and charitable surgical centres within outpatient care. A service’s location outside a public hospital does not, by itself, reveal its insurance arrangements or the patient’s eventual bill. [s1]

A policy analysis published in 2021 found that insurance expansion had improved coverage while leaving significant financial-protection problems. In particular, the gap between public and private tariffs exposed patients using private services to additional expenditure. This is a historical finding about financing mechanisms, not a quotation of current charges or a statement that every insured patient faces the same payment. [s2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12939-020-01372-4)

content.heading: Understanding the branches
content.content:
This directory separates services by their main function. Clinics concern consultations and outpatient treatment; surgical centres concern procedures; laboratories and imaging centres concern different forms of diagnostic investigation. Rehabilitation and home care extend the view beyond the initial consultation or hospital episode. WHO’s pathway framework supports reading these services as connected parts of care, while leaving room for different provider arrangements. The categories are navigation aids rather than a verified legal classification of facilities. [s1]

The distinction matters when assessing capacity. A count of consultation sites cannot describe the availability of imaging, rehabilitation, or follow-up. Nor does an insurance enrolment figure establish that every service is locally available or financially protected. The financing analysis emphasizes that population coverage, benefits, and protection against costs are separate dimensions of universal health coverage. [s2]

content.heading: Availability differs across places
content.content:
The Commonwealth Fund’s Iran profile describes an important private-sector role in urban specialist care and regional disparities in specialist distribution. It also identifies financial and nonfinancial barriers affecting access, including geography and physical accessibility. Consequently, a national description of available specialties should not be interpreted as evidence that the same services can be reached equally easily from every community. [s3](https://www.commonwealthfund.org/international-health-policy-center/countries/iran)

For international readers, this makes local context essential to understanding the service system. The relevant questions include the provider’s location, the kind of care offered, its relationship to other services, and the financing arrangements described by the applicable institution. This page explains the system rather than recommending individual providers or establishing eligibility for treatment. [s3]

content.heading: Quality includes the experience of care
content.content:
Service quality also concerns what happens around the clinical encounter. A systematic review of Iranian hospital outpatient services identified responsiveness as a particular weakness and discussed timely attention, courteous interaction, and attention to patients’ needs. Its findings concern the studies it combined, rather than a current national rating of all medical services. [s4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12913-023-09506-4)

The useful starting point is therefore a connected view: consultations, investigations, treatment, and follow-up must be understood together with affordability and access. The available research supports that framework, but a fuller account still requires service-specific evidence on rehabilitation, home care, diagnostics, and contemporary operating conditions.

name: Clinics
description: Clinics form part of Iran’s outpatient service network alongside hospital departments and independent practices. Understanding their role requires distinguishing the services offered, the organization operating them, and the arrangements used to pay for care.

seo.title: Clinics and Outpatient Care in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand clinics within Iran’s outpatient network, including ownership, financial protection, patient experience, and research limitations.

content.heading: Several settings for outpatient care
content.content:
A clinic is one setting within a wider outpatient network. WHO’s Iran assessment lists clinics and polyclinics alongside hospital services and independent practitioners. These facilities operate across public, private, and Social Security Organization arrangements. A clinic should therefore not automatically be understood as privately owned, and an outpatient consultation does not necessarily take place in a stand-alone building. [s1](https://www.ccpsh.org/sites/default/files/uploaded_files/2025-10/PSE%2520in%2520I.R.%2520Iran-eng.pdf)

The Social Security Organization, an employment-linked social insurance institution, has its own clinics and polyclinics as well as arrangements to purchase care. This illustrates why ownership and financing need separate explanations: the organization delivering a consultation may also operate an insurance scheme, or it may receive payment through a contract with another institution. [s1]

content.heading: Insurance does not settle every cost
content.content:
Clinic access has an important financial dimension. A 2021 policy analysis identified the difference between public and private tariffs as a source of out-of-pocket expenditure, particularly because private providers have a substantial outpatient role. Its discussion shows why holding insurance and receiving full financial protection are different matters. [s2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12939-020-01372-4)

Those findings describe the period examined by the researchers. They do not establish a current copayment, a universal clinic fee, or the benefits available under a particular policy. For explanatory purposes, the key distinction is between the provider’s charge and the amount an insurer recognizes or reimburses. A complete contemporary account would need verified tariff schedules and contract terms rather than a single national price. [s2]

content.heading: What research can establish about quality
content.content:
Research on hospital outpatient services offers evidence about the consultation experience, but its scope needs care. A systematic review published in 2023 compared patients’ perceptions with their expectations and identified responsiveness as a weak dimension. The authors emphasized prompt service, courteous interaction, and attention to patients’ needs. These findings concern patient-reported service experience; they are not a direct measurement of diagnostic accuracy or treatment safety. [s3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12913-023-09506-4)

The review also reported substantial differences between the studies it combined, related to their populations and settings. Its results should therefore not be turned into a league table of Iranian clinics or a rating applied to an individual facility. Hospital outpatient evidence cannot automatically stand for independent practices or every kind of community clinic. [s3]

content.heading: Understanding a clinic’s place in care
content.content:
The most useful account of a clinic identifies what consultations it provides, who operates it, and how its patients connect with investigations or further treatment. WHO’s service-pathway framework places outpatient care within a broader sequence that includes hospitals and follow-up. This makes continuity an important part of understanding the setting, alongside the consultation itself. [s1]

The evidence supports a mixed outpatient landscape rather than one standardized clinic model. More detailed coverage requires a verified contemporary distinction between facility types and their permitted services. Until that evidence is available, this page remains an introduction rather than a directory or a comprehensive guide to clinic regulation.
